analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, sale, and private possession of handguns, with exceptions for police, military, security guards, and licensed target clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill had a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, never got a committee or floor vote, and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to make, sell, buy, or own a handgun or handgun ammunition. Exceptions were written for the armed forces, law enforcement agencies, registered security guard companies, and licensed target-shooting clubs whose guns are stored on club premises. People could turn in handguns to police and get paid at least $25 per gun; after a 180-day grace period, remaining private possession would carry up to five years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by handgun violence, under the bill's stated rationale: its findings cite record handgun homicide rates and an estimated $20.4 billion in annual costs from medical spending and lost productivity. Police and the military would keep their weapons; target shooters could continue only through licensed clubs with secure storage.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that handgun homicides set new records every year after 1987 and that handguns play a disproportionate role in violent crime and accidental death compared with rifles and shotguns [S3].

Its findings put the annual cost of handgun violence at $20.4 billion from direct medical expenditures and lost productivity, a burden the bill says falls on the health care system and the economy [S3].

It authorizes voluntary handgun buybacks: anyone could deliver a handgun to a designated law enforcement agency and receive the greater of $25 or fair market value, with no criminal penalty for surrendering a gun after the grace period [S3].
It requires loss and theft reporting and recordkeeping by any entity still allowed to deal in handguns, and provides forfeiture of guns used in crimes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of handgun owners, who would have to surrender their guns (for at least $25 each), face a civil penalty of up to $500 after the grace period, or risk criminal possession charges. Handgun makers, importers, and dealers would lose nearly all civilian sales, keeping only business from police, military, security firms, and clubs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: The bill would criminalize possession by a very large lawful population overnight: its own findings count more than 75 million privately held handguns as of 1995, and private owners outside the exceptions would face up to five years in prison for possessing a gun they legally bought before the ban [S3].

The buyback terms are weak compensation: a person surrendering a handgun more than 180 days after enactment pays a civil penalty of up to $500 and receives no payment, and even during the grace period a valuable collector's gun is reimbursed at a value set by the Treasury Secretary [S3].

A prohibition on a widely owned consumer product raises serious enforcement and constitutional questions the bill does not resolve, and bans that are difficult to enforce can push sales into illegal markets while leaving the underlying supply in circulation; the bill does not address the existing stock of tens of millions of guns beyond voluntary surrender [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's public-health case, record handgun homicides and billions in annual costs, is stated in its own findings, and the exceptions for police, military, and licensed clubs show an attempt to spare legitimate uses. But the costs are heavy and fall on a huge population: tens of millions of owners would lose property worth far more than the $25 minimum buyback payment, and a ban of this scale would be extremely hard to enforce against the existing gun stock. It was a maximal proposal with no apparent coalition behind it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never came up for any vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the bill on February 13, 1997 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On March 5, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, where no further action was recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun owners and the firearms industry are better off because the bill died: no civilian handgun sales or possession were restricted, and no buyback or licensing regime was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the handgun prohibition bill; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Crime on March 5, 1997, and never reported it out or scheduled any markup or vote for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action; the bill died there when the 105th Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the only sign of support was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.note: The bill bans all civilian handgun transactions, leaving manufacturers and dealers with sales only to the military, law enforcement, security firms, and licensed clubs — a fraction of the market. Under the bill's premise, their civilian sales revenue is the channel through which guns reach the violence the bill targets.

Security companies keep the right to arm their guards under a $50 annual Treasury registration with storage and recordkeeping rules, becoming one of the few private channels allowed to possess handguns.

Licensed handgun clubs become the only way a private citizen can keep a handgun, stored at the club or a police facility, under a $25 annual license and strict supervision rules — locking in the club model as the survivor of the ban.
